title: Behavior of Square-Round Shaft Combination Helical Piles and Anchors
summary: Explore how Combo helical piles pair square-shaft leads with round-shaft extensions to improve installation, stability, and axial capacity in varied soils.
body_markdown:
Historically, most helical anchors and piles have been fabricated with helices attached to either a solid square or open pipe central shaft (Square-Shaft (SS) or Round-Shaft (RS)). This is generally how most manufacturers around the world have supplied these elements although in some cases a tubular square shaft or solid round bar are also used for small anchors.


## Square Shaft vs. Round (Pipe) Shaft Helical Piles


Square shafts


are more frequently used for tension loading while round shafts


are more commonly used for compression loading. For the same helix configuration, a square-shaft anchor or pile requires less installation torque than a comparable round-shaft anchor or pile and typically gives a somewhat lower axial load capacity.


In some soils, a round-shaft helical anchor or pile may “spin-out” during installation as a large portion of the installation energy is engaged in overcoming the shaft resistance developed between the helical plates and above the top helix. This can occur even if a large crowd force is used during installation. In some geologic profiles, such as stiff glacial clays, marls or highly weathered argillaceous bedrock, initial advance of a square-shaft section is typically more successful that a round-shaft lead section.


Here is a generalized overview of the difference between these two shaft types:


**Square Shaft** **Round (Pipe) Shaft**


More frequently used for tension loading


More commonly used for compression loading


Requires less installation torque


Generally requires more installation torque


Typically gives a somewhat lower axial load capacity


Typically higher axial load capacity


Highest torque correlation factor (Kt) May "spin out" during installation


Better penetration in dense soil Less likely to buckle in soft soils


Generally lower cost per kip


## Combining the Best of Both Piles


Each pile type has its advantages - with the installation advantages of the square shaft and the axial capacity and stiffness advantages of the round shaft - so the idea of *combining* their advantages was born and cleverly named the Chance "Combo Pile."


A Combo pile consists of:


1.


1) a traditional square-shaft (SS) lead section that could have 1, 2 or 3 helices;


2.


2) a transition fixture (square-to-round shaft); and


3.


3) round-shaft (RS) extensions which could have additional helices or could be just a plain round shaft.


Once the square-shaft lead section advances, the round-shaft section can usually advance without difficulty, aided by the rotation of the lead section. The combination of a square-shaft lead helical section with one or more following round-shaft sections can give some advantages over either a square-shaft or round-shaft anchor or pile on its own. The transition from a square-shaft lead section to round-shaft extension sections is possible using a unique cast fixture manufactured by Chance Civil Construction creating a combination or Combo pile, Figure 1.


Commonly, Combo Piles for many applications consist of an SS150 (1.5 in. x 1.5 in. solid square bar) lead to RS2875 (2-7/8 in. hollow pipe) extension or SS175 (1.75 in. x 1.75 in.) lead to RS3500 extension, although other combinations are available as shown in Table 1.

## Lessons on Installation Torque from Load Testing


Let’s take a look at some results of some full-scale field tests on Combo piles in comparison to traditional SS and RS piles.


Tests were performed at two sites in western Massachusetts:


-


-


at Site-1


the soils consisted of stiff clay overlying soft clay;


-


at Site-2


the soils consisted of medium dense silty sand overlying stiff clay.


Three different piles were tested at each site. The same helix configuration, three helices with 8-, 10-, and 12-inch diameters, was used on all three lead sections:


-


-


[Square Shaft pile](https://www.hubbell.com/chancefoundationsolutions/en/products/1-5-square-shaft-lead-ss5-bldg-code-81012-x-5ft/p/278597)


- 1-1/2" solid square shaft lead section (SS5) with 3 helices of 8", 10" and 12" diameters followed by plain SS5 extension sections


- [Round Shaft pile](https://www.hubbell.com/chancefoundationsolutions/en/products/2-875-round-shaft-lead-rs2875-203-bldg-code-81012-x-5ft/p/278450)


- 2-7/8" hollow round shaft lead section (RS2875) with 3 helices of 8", 10" and 12" diameters followed by plain RS2875 extension sections


-


Combo piles - 1-1/2" solid square shaft lead section (SS5) with 3 helices of 8", 10" and 12" diameters followed by a


[C1500896](https://www.hubbell.com/chancefoundationsolutions/en/products/transition-coupler-ss150-to-rs2875-combo-pile/p/278622)


transition coupler and transitioned to


plain RS2875 extension sections.


In the upper stiff clay, RS torque is highest because of the higher torque developed in the round lead section. In the lower soft clay, there is little difference in all three sections because the undrained shear strength is so low. It should be no surprise that the installation torque of the round-shaft sections is higher than comparable square-shaft sections with the same configuration of helices. Throughout the profile at this site, the SS and Combo piles have nearly the same installation torque. For square-shaft anchors and piles, most of the installation energy is engaged in advancing the helical plates.


Figure 2. Installation Torque for SS5, RS2875 and Combo Piles in Stiff Clay and Soft Clay Massachusetts Site 1.


Figure 3 shows a comparison between the measured installation torque of an SS, RS and Combo pile with the same helix configuration installed in a medium dense sand overlying stiff clay. In this case there is considerable difference in installation torque between the three piles throughout the upper sand (down to about 15 ft. where the clay is encountered) and then the three piles show similar torque.


Figure 3. Installation Torque for SS5, RS2875 and Combo Piles in Sand and Stiff Clay Massachusetts Site 2.


Axial capacity of Combo piles generally falls in between that of square-shaft and round-shaft piles, as one might expect, although based on a large number of tests at several different sites, there is no consistent trend. Torque-to-Capacity (KT) factors for Combo piles are actually similar to default values for comparable size round-shafts recommended by AC358. Data from full-scale field testing of Combo piles/anchors in both clay and sand show that the axial load capacity of Combo piles/anchors is generally greater than square-shaft piles/anchors but slightly less than round-shaft piles/anchors.


## Axial Load Capacity - Massachusetts Sites


Table 2 gives a summary of test results from the two Massachusetts sites. In general, the axial capacity of Combo piles falls in between SS and RS which is expected. Higher axial capacity from the RS anchors is consistent with higher installation torques shown in Figures 2 and 3. It may also be of interest to note that the displacement at 50% of the ultimate axial capacity (i.e., Q10/2 ; F.S. = 2) is very low, all less than ½ in. This is one of the advantages of using helical anchors and piles; small displacement at working load.

## Conclusions on Axial Load Capacity by Pile Type


Careful evaluation of these tests shows that:


1. In nearly every case, axial capacity in compression is higher than axial capacity in tension


, and in some case by as much as a factor of 2.


2. In almost every case, for both tension and compression, the axial capacity of the Combo anchors/piles falls in between SS and RS anchors/piles


. This is consistent with the results presented in Table 2 for the Massachusetts sites.


3. The increase in axial capacity of a Combo anchor or pile over an SS anchor/pile is the result of being able to install the Combo pile and the RS extension section following the installation of the lead SS section.


4. The difference in axial capacity between a single-helix and double-helix anchor or pile is approximately proportional to the ratio of cross-sectional area of the helices.


5. It's also interesting to note that the displacement at a Factor-of-Safety of 2 (Q10/2) of all these tests is less than 0.50 in. and averages about 0.33 in.


## Summary


Recent field test results show that in cases where the stratigraphy may not readily allow the installation of a round-shaft helical anchor or pile or the installation may be difficult, a Combo anchor or pile consisting of an SS lead helical section followed by RS extension sections can overcome this issue. Axial load capacity of Combo anchors and piles falls in between capacity of SS and RS anchors and piles with the same helix geometry.


Round-shaft extension sections used in combination with square-shaft lead sections generally give increased stability against lateral buckling under compression loading or when the shaft extends above the ground surface. If additional bucking resistance is needed, the round-shaft section could be filled with grout. Additionally, the pipe shaft extensions give higher lateral capacity as compared to a square-shaft section which can be very important in cases where the shaft extends above ground, for example when used as ground-mount solar systems.


*Dr. Alan Lutenegger is Emeritus Professor of Geotechnical Engineering at the University of Massachusetts-Amherst. He has over 45 years of experience in geotechnical engineering and over 20 years of practical experience with helical anchors and piles.*
